The Andean pygmy owl (Glaucidium jardinii) exhibits a comparatively fast life history among Neotropical Strigidae, particularly in the developmental schedule of its altricial nestlings. Eggs incubated at a temperature of approximately 30 °C [T = 30 °C] hatch after a period of about 28 days [ab = about 28 days], an incubation duration that aligns closely with estimates from the closely related Glaucidium nana and reflects the typical energetic constraints of small-bodied, cavity-nesting raptors. Hatchlings emerge at a relatively modest weight; based on allometric relationships derived from congeneric species such as Glaucidium nana, the initial wet weight at hatching is estimated at 8.8 grams [Ww0 = 8.8 grams]. This low neonatal mass is consistent with the altricial mode of development common to small owls, where significant somatic growth and feather development occur during an extended post-hatching nestling period under intense biparental care.

Following hatching, the nestling phase is characterized by rapid somatic growth and feather maturation under the thermal conditions of the nest cavity. Under the active metabolic temperatures typical of this stage, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time since hatching at fledging is approximately 28.5 days [tx = approximately 28.5 days], a value again drawn from comparative data for Glaucidium nana. During this period, the developing chick progresses from an entirely dependent, downy neonate to a fully feathered fledgling capable of short, sustained flights, driven by a high basal metabolic rate that supports the energetic costs of tissue synthesis and thermoregulation.

The basal metabolic rate of adult Andean pygmy owls has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions, providing insight into the energetic costs of endothermy at rest. At a stable body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the resting oxygen consumption, measured as the maximum basal metabolic rate, reaches 123.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 123.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, obtained from respirometry trials, is characteristic of a small, active avian predator with a high mass-specific metabolic demand, reflecting the energetic premium placed on maintaining homeothermy and rapid digestive processing of vertebrate prey in cool, montane environments.

Sexual maturation in this species unfolds as a discrete physiological transition that subsequently enables the initiation of breeding. Under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], puberty is attained relatively late relative to the nestling period: the time since birth at puberty is 78 days [tp = 78 days]. This interval from hatching to gonadal development suggests a post-fledging period of continued somatic growth and social integration before the reproductive system becomes fully responsive to hormonal cues. Following maturation, the first breeding event typically occurs considerably later, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at 657 days [tR = 657 days] under these same thermal conditions, a delay that likely reflects the challenges of territory establishment and mate acquisition in high-altitude paramo habitats.

The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 66.725 grams [Wwi = 66.725 grams], a figure supported by field measurements from the species' range which document a broader interval of 54.9 to 77.4 grams for adult females. Reproductive output is modest and paced to the constraints of a high-altitude environment: females typically lay 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch] and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild, assessed under the ambient thermal conditions typical of their active period at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 7.6 years [am = approximately 7.6 years], a lifespan that balances the elevated metabolic costs of endothermy against the low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by a predatory lifestyle and low annual reproductive output.
